name: AP Drawing
overview: AP Drawing is a portfolio course with no sit-down exam. Students develop a body of work through an inquiry-guided Sustained Investigation and present Selected Works that demonstrate drawing skills: mark-making, line quality, surface manipulation, the illusion of depth and space, light and shade, and composition, using elements and principles of art and design. Students may work in many media, including graphite, charcoal, ink, pastel, colored pencil, painting, printmaking, digital drawing, and mixed media.
examMode: Portfolio submitted through the AP Digital Portfolio (no sit-down exam)

sections.name: Section 1
sections.notes: 15 digital images (some may be details or process images) with typed responses describing the questions that guided the investigation and how the work shows practice, experimentation, and revision; each image is identified with materials, processes, and size.

sections.name: Section 2
sections.notes: Digital images of 5 works, each identified with the ideas, materials, and processes used. Works may also appear in the Sustained Investigation.

skills.name: Inquiry
skills.description: Ask questions that guide a sustained investigation of materials, processes, and ideas.

skills.name: Practice, experimentation, and revision
skills.description: Develop work over time, try alternatives, and revise based on reflection and feedback.

skills.name: Materials, processes, and ideas
skills.description: Make intentional choices of media and techniques to communicate ideas.

skills.name: Skill synthesis
skills.description: Demonstrate drawing skills with control and purpose.

skills.name: Written evidence
skills.description: Describe inquiry, process, and choices clearly and concisely.

scoring.summary: Trained AP readers score the portfolio with rubrics. The Sustained Investigation (60%) is evaluated on the inquiry, evidence of practice, experimentation, and revision, synthesis of materials, processes, and ideas, and skill. Selected Works (40%) is evaluated on skill and on how materials, processes, and ideas are used and described. Klutch's practice tasks use simplified 4-point scales.

frqTypes.name: Written evidence task
frqTypes.howScored: Klutch practice scale: specificity, connection to the inquiry, evidence of process, and clarity within the character limits.

frqTypes.name: Portfolio planning task
frqTypes.howScored: Klutch practice scale: specific steps, connection to the inquiry, evidence of experimentation and revision, and realistic scope.

strategy: Start with a question you genuinely care about, specific enough to guide choices but open enough to sustain 15 images.
Document process as you go: photograph sketches, experiments, and revisions, not just finished pieces.
Let each work respond to what you learned from the previous one; show the investigation evolving.
Write concrete statements: name techniques, materials, and decisions instead of vague words like 'explore' and 'express'.
Choose Selected Works that show your strongest skill and the clearest relationship among materials, processes, and ideas.
Photograph work in even light, crop cleanly, and include details that reveal technique.
pitfalls: A sustained investigation that is really a collection of unrelated works.
Statements that describe the subject but not the inquiry or the process.
Poor photographs that hide the quality of the work.
Using references or tools in ways that break AP policy; transform references significantly and follow the current AI policy.
caveats: A new artificial intelligence policy applies to 2026-27 portfolios; read the current AP Art and Design guidelines on AP Central before using any AI tools or digital references.

Check the current character limits for each written response in the AP Digital Portfolio; historically, Sustained Investigation responses have allowed up to 600 characters each and identifying information up to 100 characters per field.
Point values on Klutch practice tasks are Klutch practice scales, not the official rubric.
